solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Spooner’s escaped scrap warning of danger

indicators.note: Dr Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of neighbouring words, so his name tells you to do the same

blocks.note: escaped is fled; it takes the opening sound of the other word
a scrap of cloth is a rag; it takes the opening sound of the other word

explanation.surface: Someone notices a fragment that got away and treats it as an alarm signal.
explanation.walkthrough: FLED RAG with the F and R sounds swapped becomes RED FLAG.
explanation.definitionFit: A crimson banner is flown as a signal of hazard, and the phrase is now used figuratively for any early sign of trouble.

clue.text: Herd topped land ahead

indicators.note: to top something is to cut off its top, and in a down clue the top is the first letter

blocks.note: land is ground, which loses its first letter
a team that is ahead is up

explanation.surface: A herd breaks out and claims the land in front of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Herd' looks like a noun but is the verb. GROUND loses its G.
explanation.definitionFit: To gather scattered cattle into one group is to drive them together, the cowboy's job on a ranch.

clue.text: Beginning university in financial hardship

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside it

blocks.note: U is the standard abbreviation for university
owing money is a financial hardship

explanation.surface: A student starting university is already short of money.
explanation.walkthrough: U goes inside DEBT.
explanation.definitionFit: A first public appearance or first outing is the start of a career, so the noun means a launch or opening.

clue.text: Not totally cool, oath so mean and vile

indicators.note: only part of the words is used, so the letters sit within a run of the clue

blocks.note: the run starts at the end of the first word and stops partway through the last

explanation.surface: A curse that falls short of cool comes across as petty and nasty.
explanation.walkthrough: cooL OATH SO MEan holds the answer across four words.
explanation.definitionFit: Something repulsive and hateful is detestable, so both words describe what causes disgust.

clue.text: Taunt about half-cut lady being unsteady

indicators.note: turned about means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards
cutting in half keeps only one half of the word

blocks.note: a dig is a jibe or taunt
the second half of this four-letter word

explanation.surface: Someone mocks a woman who is tipsy and staggering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-cut' means drunk in British slang, fitting the unsteady lady, but here it slices LADY to DY.
explanation.definitionFit: Dizzy and likely to fall, the adjective describes a person who cannot keep their balance.

clue.text: Bloke supposing that revolutionary cold and evil

indicators.note: a revolution turns something round, so the letters face the other way

blocks.note: a bloke is a man
if means supposing that
C is cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A man imagines a radical who is chilly and wicked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' reads as a noun for a rebel, but it turns IF round.
explanation.definitionFit: A literary adjective for something causing harm or malevolent, from the Latin for wrongdoing.

clue.text: Home and dry after swimming, leaving behind hard current

indicators.note: to leave something behind is to go without it, so a letter is dropped
something swimming is moving about loosely, so the letters drift into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
H is the pencil abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A swimmer gets out, dries off and heads home, leaving a strong current behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' looks like the river's flow in the swimming picture, but it is the definition. Drop H from HOMEANDDRY and rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Belonging to the present time, contemporary, is what current means as an adjective.

clue.text: Swellings from cycling fall

indicators.note: going round in a cycle moves the first letter to the back

blocks.note: a slump is a fall, as in prices

explanation.surface: Bruises and bumps from tumbling off a bicycle.
explanation.walkthrough: The S at the front of SLUMP rides round to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Bumps or raised areas on the body are protuberances, so the plural nouns match.

clue.text: Simple housing is erected with mass reproduction

indicators.note: to house something is to give it a place inside
in a down clue, putting something up makes it read from bottom to top

blocks.note: facile means simple or easy
taken as written
M is the abbreviation for mass in physics

explanation.surface: Basic prefab homes going up fast through mass production.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'erected' turns IS upside down; the surface's mass production is a hint at the definition's sense of copying.
explanation.definitionFit: An exact copy of a document or object is a replica, so the two nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Knowing about eastern end of lair containing factory

indicators.note: to be about something is to be around it, so one piece goes round the other
the end of a word is its final letter

blocks.note: canny means shrewd or knowing
E is the abbreviation for eastern
the final letter of this word

explanation.surface: Someone shrewd about the far end of a den that houses a works.
explanation.walkthrough: E and R go inside CANNY. 'Containing' looks like a container signal, but it belongs to the definition: a factory that puts food in containers.
explanation.definitionFit: A plant where food is sealed in tins is a factory whose whole job is packing produce into metal containers.

clue.text: Generic article of French striped clothing ultimate in menswear

indicators.note: clothing something wraps it, so one piece goes around another
the ultimate is the last, so only the final letter is taken

blocks.note: un is the French indefinite article
banded means marked with stripes
the final letter of this word

explanation.surface: A plain item of French stripy clothing completing a men's outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' suggests a garment but means a grammatical article; R goes inside BANDED.
explanation.definitionFit: Generic goods are sold without a company label or trademark, so the two adjectives match.

clue.text: Covering over wine

blocks.note: a mac is a raincoat, a covering
on top of is over

explanation.surface: Something placed on top of a drink, like a cloth over wine.
explanation.walkthrough: A mac is the British short name for a mackintosh raincoat.
explanation.definitionFit: Mâcon is a Burgundy region whose white and red vintages carry the town's name, a classic French appellation.

clue.text: Lose tongue after one replaces you reportedly

indicators.note: to replace is to take another's place, so one letter is swapped for another
something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so it is heard rather than seen

blocks.note: a tongue is a language, here that of the Netherlands
I is the Roman numeral one
the letter U is pronounced like this word

explanation.surface: Someone loses their voice after being replaced by another.
explanation.walkthrough: In DUTCH, I takes the place of U.
explanation.definitionFit: To ditch something is to get rid of or abandon it, so the verbs share the sense of discarding.

clue.text: I say shirker should move region

indicators.note: letters told to move change position, so they are rearranged

blocks.note: oy is an exclamation calling for attention, like I say
taken as written

explanation.surface: A boss tells the idle worker to transfer to another area.
explanation.walkthrough: YORKSHIRE is a large county in northern England. 'I say' reads as a speaker's aside, but it supplies OY.
explanation.definitionFit: The historic English county is a large area of the north, so it is an example of a region.

clue.text: Played backing Queen as decided beforehand

indicators.note: moving backwards in an across clue makes the letters read right to left

blocks.note: to play a piece is to perform it; the regal pair in its middle is lifted out to be turned
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword queen

explanation.surface: A band performed as backing group for Queen, as arranged in advance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Queen' and 'backing' suggest the rock band and its session musicians, but the Queen is the ER already inside the word for played, and backing turns it round in place.
explanation.definitionFit: Formed in advance, as an opinion settled before the facts are known, so the participle means determined ahead of time.

clue.text: Help this gang struggling to get rogue elephant

indicators.note: something struggling is twisting about, so the combined letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written; this is what the jumble must produce

explanation.surface: Keepers call for assistance as their team wrestles a dangerous elephant.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: HELP plus the answer ('this') jumbled makes ROGUE ELEPHANT, so take HELP out of ROGUE ELEPHANT and rearrange the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A group of attendants or hangers-on around a celebrity is a retinue, which can loosely be called a gang.

clue.text: Villain having brief laugh being introduced to source of money

indicators.note: something brief is cut short, so the last letter goes
something introduced to another is put into it

blocks.note: the mint is where coins are made
a scream is something hilarious, a real laugh

explanation.surface: A crook gives a short laugh on meeting the person bankrolling him.
explanation.walkthrough: A scream is informal for something hilarious; the Royal Mint is where British coins are made, hence the source of money.
explanation.definitionFit: A wrongdoer or scoundrel is a person who behaves badly, so the two nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Thorny plant, say, covering home

indicators.note: to cover something is to go over and around it

blocks.note: a plant is an infiltrator, and 'say' flags it as an example
being in is being at home

explanation.surface: A prickly shrub growing over a house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' looks botanical beside 'Thorny', but it means an undercover agent; 'say' marks it as an example of one.
explanation.definitionFit: Covered in prickles or sharp points, the two adjectives describe the same kind of stem or skin.

clue.text: Many unburden

blocks.note: first meaning: a great quantity, British slang
second meaning, split in two: to cast off weights carried

explanation.walkthrough: Read as one word it is British slang for a large amount; split as two words it means to drop what you are carrying.
explanation.definitionFit: The slang noun means lots of something, and the two-word phrase means getting rid of cargo or weight.

clue.text: King wearing child’s headwear

indicators.note: someone wearing something has it around them, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: a mite is a small child
R is Rex, king

explanation.surface: A monarch putting on his child's hat.
explanation.walkthrough: The child wears the king: R goes inside MITE.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall pointed ceremonial hat worn by bishops is a kind of hat, so the noun fits.

clue.text: Accidents and risk exposed by hospital shown in charts

indicators.note: to expose something is to strip its outer covering, so the outside letters go
something shown in another appears inside it

blocks.note: maps are charts
this word with its outer letters stripped
H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs

explanation.surface: Injury figures and danger levels revealed by a hospital in its graphs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exposed' reads as being at risk, but it means stripping the outer letters off the word risk.
explanation.definitionFit: Unlucky events or slips that cause harm are misfortunes, so the plural nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Dull hearing step class not on

indicators.note: by hearing we take in what is said, so the word is judged by its sound
not having something means it is taken away

blocks.note: a stile is a step over a fence
a class is a lesson
taken as written, then removed

explanation.surface: A tedious aerobics class, heard about without enthusiasm.
explanation.walkthrough: A stile is a set of steps for climbing over a fence or wall, common on British footpaths. LESSON without ON leaves LESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking flair or elegance makes something drab and uninteresting, so the adjectives are close synonyms.

clue.text: Small tick observed after removing lead holding a dog

indicators.note: the lead is the front, so its first letter is taken off
to hold something is to keep it within

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small
taken as written
a tick and a mo are both a brief moment
eyed means looked at, observed

explanation.surface: A vet spots a tiny parasite once a dog's leash is off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tick' and 'lead' look like a parasite and a leash in the dog picture; they are a moment and a first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A Samoyed is a fluffy white Siberian breed of spitz, so it is an example of the animal.

clue.text: Son given unwanted responsibility was inattentive

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for son
to be lumbered with something is to be stuck with a burden

explanation.surface: A boy saddled with chores he did not want drifted off and paid no attention.
explanation.walkthrough: Lumbered is British usage for being landed with an unwelcome task.
explanation.definitionFit: Dozing or sleeping means not paying attention, so slept is a figurative sense of failed to notice.

clue.text: Seeing that dog going up wood

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: as means seeing that, since
a lab is a Labrador retriever

explanation.surface: Watching a dog climb into the trees.
explanation.walkthrough: AS then LAB, all read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Balsa is the very light timber of a tropical American tree, used for model aircraft, so it is a kind of timber.

clue.text: Old saw

blocks.note: first meaning: old-fashioned, out of date
second meaning: went out with romantically

explanation.walkthrough: 'Old saw' looks like a set phrase for a proverb; the words are two separate meanings, an adjective and a past-tense verb.
explanation.definitionFit: An adjective for something no longer fashionable, and the past tense of a verb for going out with someone romantically.

clue.text: Sub‘s sign of hesitancy after pass back

indicators.note: going back in an across clue reads right to left

blocks.note: a col is a mountain pass
um is the sound of someone hesitating

explanation.surface: A substitute footballer hesitates after a back pass.
explanation.walkthrough: A locum is a stand-in doctor or vicar, a British usage.
explanation.definitionFit: A temporary replacement filling in for a professional is a substitute, so the nouns match.

clue.text: Retired Cockney player discussed England footballer

indicators.note: something discussed is talked about, so it is judged by sound

blocks.note: Harry Kane captained England's football team

explanation.surface: A retired London actor chats about an England striker.
explanation.walkthrough: Michael Caine is a Londoner and famous actor who has retired from films; 'player' means actor, not a sportsman.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Michael, born in south London, is the most famous screen star with a Cockney accent, and he announced his retirement from acting.

clue.text: Article with reportedly obscure use

indicators.note: what is reported is passed on by mouth, so the sound counts, not the spelling

blocks.note: a is the indefinite article
to veil something is to obscure it

explanation.surface: A rumour that a news item has some vague purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: VEIL is respelt to match its sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Of no avail means of no use, so the noun means benefit or advantage.

clue.text: Game with such realism recreated Guatemala City

indicators.note: to recreate is to make again in a new form, so the letters are rebuilt

blocks.note: taken as written
stands in for the answer itself, the realism that joins the game in the mix
taken as written; this is what the jumble must produce

explanation.surface: A video game rebuilt the Central American capital in lifelike detail.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: GAME plus the answer ('such realism') rearranged gives GUATEMALA CITY, so take GAME out of it and rearrange the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Being true to life is a matter of real existence, so faithfulness to fact is close to the noun.

clue.text: Name of man we recalled opening boxes

indicators.note: to call something back sends it the other way
to box something is to enclose it

blocks.note: an opening is a start
taken as written

explanation.surface: The man's name we remembered, as boxing opened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boxes' looks like a sport or a noun, but it is the verb for enclosing.
explanation.definitionFit: Stewart is a common Scottish forename for a boy, so it is one example of a male name.

clue.text: Sink key in hole and door’s opening

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it
the opening of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: Esc is the escape key on a keyboard
a den is a hole or lair
the first letter of this word

explanation.surface: Plumbing jobs: a sink, a key in a lock hole, and a door gap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sink' looks like a kitchen basin, but it is a verb; the key is a computer keyboard's escape key, not one for a lock.
explanation.definitionFit: To go down or drop lower is to sink, so the verbs mean moving downwards.
